column6: Late Archaic communities occupied the Ortoire shell-midden complex, the type site from which the archaeological name “Ortoiroid” was derived.

Saladoid communities established settlements in Trinidad and produced distinctive ceramics. The earliest local expression is known as the Cedros complex; it later developed into the more widespread Palo Seco complex.
column9: Boomert, Faber-Morse and Rouse (2013), The 1946 and 1953 Yale University Excavations in Trinidad, Yale University Publications in Anthropology 92

column6: Barrancoid ceramic traditions from the Lower Orinoco became integrated with Trinidad’s existing Late Palo Seco tradition. Both pottery traditions were made and used together, suggesting exchange, coexistence and likely intermarriage.
A new local ceramic complex developed through interaction between Trinidad and Arauquinoid communities of the Lower Orinoco. Bontour pottery was generally shell-tempered and minimally decorated.
Bontour settlements became widespread along the coast and inland, indicating increasing population density and island-wide exchange.

The Mayoid ceramic tradition reached Trinidad from the Guiana coastal region several centuries before European contact. It overlapped with the older Bontour complex and featured thin-walled bowls and necked jars with minimal decoration.
